history.content: What is Cassava brown streak virus and how can I manage it?

Then, for the next planting, cut only from plants that look healthy, with normal green leaves and no leaf deformation. Use an improved tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep the stand uniform and well fed. If you need clean cuttings, ITRA can provide them.

history.content: My cassava shows yellow blotches along the leaf veins and I think it is cassava mosaic disease, but I also see brown corky rot in the roots. What actions should I take?

draws.answer: Brown corky rot in the roots together with yellow or pale streaks along the leaf veins points to cassava bacterial blight, not cassava mosaic disease. Use only cuttings from cassava that are free of any bacterial blight symptoms. Remove and destroy any cassava plants that display the bacterial blight signs. Disinfect each tool you use before you work on the next cassava plant. Plant a cassava variety that is resistant to cassava bacterial blight for the next cycle. If you need clean resistant cuttings, go to ITRA or a registered producer, and you can ask ICAT to confirm the diagnosis.

The symptoms you describe are not cassava mosaic disease, they are bacterial blight caused by Xanthomonas axonopodis pv. manihotis. First, use cuttings only from healthy plants. Second, remove and destroy any infected plants you find. Third, disinfect your tools between each plant. Fourth, plant a resistant cassava variety in the cleared area. Fifth, rotate the plot to reduce future disease risk. See ITRA or a registered producer for clean resistant cuttings.

per_item.reference: Stop all movement of animals in and out of your herd immediately. Isolate every sick goat or sheep at once, keeping them away from healthy ones. Do not sell or slaughter any animal while the outbreak lasts, and dispose of any dead carcasses safely. Give the sick animals clean water and soft feed to keep them comfortable. On veterinary advice, vaccinate all healthy and in-contact animals with the PPR vaccine. Notify the veterinary service IMMEDIATELY.

history.content: movement restriction during outbreak now

draws.answer: Stop all new movements of healthy animals and all animal transport without a validated vector control plan. First, isolate every animal showing high fever, red or purple blotches, or bloody diarrhoea and kill or burn them. Then destroy any dead animals by burying or burning them, and do not sell or give away any animal. Remove and disinfect any tainted bedding and take dead animals to a veterinary service for proper disposal. Keep these steps in place for the rest of the grazing season. If you need help with a vaccination or disinfection, see ICAT quickly.

Movement restriction remains the key measure right now. Confine your animals and stop all trading in or out of the area. Dispose of dead animals by burying or burning and do not sell or eat them. Clean the pen thoroughly and install a footbath at the entrance. Do not travel with your herd. Notify the veterinary service immediately for further instructions.

per_item.reference: That purple weed is Striga affecting sorghum. First, pull the Striga by hand before it flowers and burn the uprooted material so the seed does not spread. Then feed the soil with organic manure plus some urea to weaken the Striga and strengthen your sorghum. Earth up the soil after you apply the nutrients. After that, rotate or intercrop the sorghum with a grain legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean to lower the seed bank. If the field is severely infested, you should see ICAT for tolerant sorghum varieties and a multi-year rotation plan.

history.content: There is a strange purple weed around the base of my sorghum and the crop is not growing well. What steps do I take?

draws.answer: The weed you see is Striga, the plant of the Sorghum vigil. First, pull out the whole plant and destroy it at ground level so the striga spores are not carried up into your sorghum tassels. Then, when the sorghum reaches tasseling, sprinkle a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each funnel of the young flower buds. This mix treats about 1,500-2,000 plants per kilogram of neem powder, which is roughly 6-8 kg for your 0.25-hectare field. Remember never to use neem powder alone because the oil can scorch the plant, so always pair it with the inert carrier. After you harvest, plan to rotate a cereal after the sorghum so the striga-fighting cereal can follow. For a proper field diagnosis and the correct variety recommendation, consult ICAT.

The weed you are seeing is striga, which reduces the yield of sorghum. Sow a striga-tolerant variety during the recommended early sowing period. When the plants reach panicle initiation, about 30-35 days after sowing, spray an approved insecticide at the labelled rate. Do not repeat the application; always use the correct rate. Before spraying, check with ICAT to confirm the current approved product and exact dose. Also, pull the striga plants out before they flower to keep the field weed-free. For the product and rate details, see ICAT.

per_item.reference: It is not cassava brown streak disease, it is cassava mosaic disease because the leaf deformation is the key sign, not the root rot. First, pull up and destroy any plants that are strongly mottled and stunted. Then, for the next planting, collect cuttings only from plants that look healthy and avoid any mottled or deformed stems. After that, plant an improved tolerant variety supplied by ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep the stand uniform and well-fed. Finally, do not move cuttings from fields that had the disease. See ITRA for clean tolerant cuttings.

history.content: My cassava plants have leaves that look pale and mottled and the leaves are twisted. I also see some brown, corky parts inside the roots after digging. Is this cassava brown streak disease?

draws.answer: Those signs are typical of cassava mosaic disease, not the brown streak disease. First, uproot and destroy the cassava plants that are heavily mottled, stunted, or have deformed leaves because no spray will cure them. Then, when you plant again, take cuttings only from cassava plants that have normal, green leaves and no distortion. Never use a cuttings piece from a mottled or deformed plant. Finally, choose a tolerant cassava variety supplied by ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep the stand uniform and well fed. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, ITRA can help you.

Yes, those symptoms are typical of cassava mosaic disease. First, uproot and destroy the strongly mottled, stunted plants because they will not recover and they keep feeding the whitefly that spreads the virus. Then, for the next planting, take cuttings only from healthy-looking plants with normal green leaves and no deformation, never from a mottled or deformed stem. Plant an improved tolerant variety that you can obtain from ITRA or a registered cutting producer. Keep the new stand uniform and well fed. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, ITRA can help you.

per_item.reference: Striga hermonthica, known locally as witchweed, should be pulled by hand before it flowers and the uprooted plants burned to stop seed spread. After removal, add organic manure together with some urea and earth up the soil to weaken the weed and boost the sorghum. Finally, rotate or intercrop sorghum with a grain legume like cowpea, groundnut or soybean to run down the seed bank. For tolerant sorghum varieties or a multi-year rotation plan on a badly infested field, go to ICAT.

history.content: What management steps are recommended for Striga hermonthica on sorghum?

draws.answer: Striga hermonthica is the parasitic weed that takes over the lodging of sorghum, and the first step is to pull it out immediately once it appears. Next, rotate your sorghum with a cereal and do not plant it on the same land for two successive years to cut the weed's spread. Plant a Tolwa or ACR97 sorghum variety that matures in 75 to 85 days when the rains are strong, usually from mid-June to early July. Do not sow on a first isolated shower; wait until the rains are reliable. For a good-storage variety, go to ICAT.

The recommended control for Striga hermonthica on sorghum is to grow a cereal on the same plot so the sorghum cannot take root from its striga plants. First, sow a line of sorghum in your field. Then, when the sorghum is at panicle initiation, pick the Striga plants that are attached to the base of the sorghum stalks. After you have harvested the sorghum, move to the next row and leave the Striga alone. If you need help choosing the right sorghum variety or determining if a spray is needed, visit ICAT.

per_item.reference: It is cassava mosaic disease because the twisted, shrunken leaves and plant stunting are the key leaf deformation signs. First, pull up and destroy the strongly mottled and stunted cassava plants. Next, for the next planting, collect cuttings only from healthy-looking cassava and never from a mottled or deformed stem. Then, plant a tolerant cassava variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep a uniform, well-fed stand. Finally, do not move cuttings from fields with symptoms. See ITRA for clean tolerant cuttings.

history.content: Leaves on my cassava are twisted and look like they are shrinking, and the plants are short. Is this cassava mosaic disease?

draws.answer: Yes, those symptoms are cassava mosaic disease. First uproot and destroy the cassava plants that are strongly mottled, stunted and have twisted, puckered leaves because they carry the virus. Then, for the next planting, cut only from cassava plants that have normal green leaves and no deformation, never from a mottled or deformed stem. Plant an improved tolerant cassava variety obtained from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep the stand uniform and well fed. This approach stops the virus from moving through cuttings. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, see ITRA.

Yes, those symptoms are cassava mosaic disease. Remove and destroy the cassava plants that show strong mottling and deformation. For the next planting, take cuttings only from cassava plants that look healthy, with even green leaves and no twisted or shrunken parts. Do not use any cuttings from a mottled or deformed stem. Plant an improved tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep a uniform, well-fed stand. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, ITRA can provide them.

Feed the soil with organic manure plus some urea and earth up to weaken Striga and strengthen the crop. Rotate or intercrop your sorghum with a grain legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean to run down the seed bank. history.content: My sorghum is not growing well and I see some strange weeds around the plants.
Do you see a purple or pink flowered weed clinging around the base of the stunted sorghum?
Yes, there are purple flowers at the base of the plants.

draws.answer: The weed is Striga, a parasitic plant that covers the sorghum roots. Do not rely on natural enemies because they are ineffective. Sow an improved sorghum variety that matures in 55-75 days when the rains are strong, usually from mid-June to early July. Weed the sorghum at 15-25 days after sowing and then repeat the weeding about 10 days later, following the schedule for your sorghum type. At harvest cut the sorghum stalks at ground level and leave the stover in the soil to feed the Nectria fungi that help the root nodules grow. After the sorghum, always plant a cereal to use the nitrogen left by the legume. For the best variety, contact ICAT.

You have groundnut rosette, which shows stunted growth with yellow or green mottling and bunched, distorted young leaves on sorghum. Do not use the same seed for the next crop; select a tolerant sorghum variety. After that, clear or bury all old groundnut residues to remove the virus carry-over. Rotate groundnut with cereals and avoid planting it on the same land year after year. For the tolerant variety, you can go to ICAT.

per_item.reference: Remove the affected plants from the field and destroy them. Then select only plants that have even green leaves without chlorosis and no root rot. Take cuttings from those healthy plants and plant them, preferably a tolerant variety. If you need help identifying the disease, bring a sample to ITRA.

history.content: I found some cassava plants with chlorosis along the leaf veins and the roots are turning brown and corky inside. Can I still use them for planting?

draws.answer: No, those cassava plants are infected with cassava bacterial blight and must not be used for planting. Remove and destroy the plants that show the disease signs. Disinfect your tools between each plant you handle. Use only cuttings from plants that have no leaf streaks or angular water-soaked spots. Plant a resistant variety and rotate the plot. For clean resistant cuttings you can go to ITRA or a registered producer, and ICAT can confirm the diagnosis.

No, those cassava plants are infected with cassava brown streak disease and should not be used for planting. First, uproot and destroy all cassava plants that show strong yellow or pale mottling, twisted or shrunken leaves, or that have brown, corky necrotic rot in the roots. Then, for the next planting season, take cuttings only from cassava plants that have even green leaves and normal shape, never from a mottled or deformed stem. Plant an improved tolerant cassava variety supplied by ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep a uniform, well-fed stand. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, ITRA can provide them.

per_item.reference: The stunting and yellow colour are caused by Striga, a parasitic weed that attaches to the roots and robs the plant. Look for a purple or pink flowered weed clinging around the base of the stunted plants. Pull the Striga by hand before it flowers and burn what you uproot so the seed does not spread. Add organic manure and some urea to the soil and earth up to weaken Striga and strengthen the crop. Rotate or intercrop with a grain legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean to run down the seed bank. For tolerant varieties and a multi-year rotation plan, see ICAT.

history.content: why sorghum stays stunted yellow

draws.answer: The yellowing you see is caused by a nitrogen shortage on soil whose organic matter has been run down by continuous cropping without returning residues, use of too much nitrogen, or a soil that no longer stores nitrogen. First, recognize the uniform pale yellow of older lower leaves while the young tops stay greener; this is hunger for nitrogen, not a disease. Second, do not buy a broad-spectrum NPK or a systemic fungicide on a merchant's word, because on depleted soil the mineral fertilizer often gives no yield gain. Third, restore organic matter first by adding manure, compost, or by leaving residues in the field rather than burning them. Fourth, plant a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. Finally, ask ICAT for a soil analysis and the correct dose for your plot.

The yellowing and stunted growth of sorghum are caused by a nitrogen shortage in soil that has lost organic matter. First, check the leaves: a uniform pale yellow on older lower leaves shows nitrogen deficiency, not a disease. Second, do not buy only a broad-spectrum NPK fertilizer or a systemic fungicide because mineral fertilizer alone often does not give a return on run-down soil. Third, add organic matter back by applying manure, compost, or leaving residues in the field instead of burning them. Fourth, plant a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the plants at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules remain in the soil. Finally, ask ICAT for a soil analysis and the correct dose for your plot before any large purchase.

per_item.reference: Do not mix two insecticides to make a spray more potent; such mixtures can burn plants, pose health hazards, or simply not work, and a higher concentration isn't necessarily more effective. Apply one approved product at the dosage stated on its label. When pests survive, consider whether the timing or the product choice is wrong rather than increasing strength. Ask ICAT which approved product fits the pest you have and the proper timing for spraying.

history.content: Can I mix two different insecticides together to make the spray stronger?

draws.answer: No, you cannot mix insecticides and no stronger combination works. Mixing creates a compound that is not made up of the ingredients, so it is not the product you are spraying, and you cannot say which part of a product is in the final product. The correct action is the one listed on the label, which is the approved product, its rate, whether it is a fungicide or a pesticide, and its rest period after spraying. Take the label to ICAT before mixing any.

No, and there is a reason why the catalogue says each one has to be named. You mix two products and you are not using the active ingredient properly, not the target. The active ingredient is listed on each one separately: urea for the maize streak virus, an approved insecticide, and for the fungus, an approved fungicide. When you combine them, you are making a new product with a dose you cannot know, and the crop cannot tell the difference. The right product and its rate come from ICAT.

Dispose of dead goats safely to prevent further spread. Give the sick goats water and soft feed to keep them hydrated. Vaccinate all healthy and in-contact goats with PPR vaccine following veterinary advice. Notify the veterinary service immediately.

history.content: My goats have a mucky discharge from their eyes and some are dying quickly. What steps must I take?

draws.answer: The problem is leucaena poisoning in your goats. First, reduce the amount of leucaena in the diet to roughly a quarter to a third of the total ration and never let it become the main feed. Then mix the leucaena with grasses and cereal crop residues so the rumen gets plenty of roughage. Introduce any changes to the feed gradually over several days. Keep clean water always available and give a mineral or salt source at all times. If the goats keep refusing food, keep drooling, or show a swollen throat, go to the veterinary service.

Those signs indicate a tick-borne disease of your goats. Contact the veterinary service today because they alone can identify whether it is gall sickness or redwater and prescribe the right drug and dose. When you talk to the vet, mention the colour of the urine; red or black points to redwater, yellow-brown without red points to gall sickness. Keep the affected goats in shade, provide clean water and avoid making them walk. Remove all visible ticks from every animal in the herd, not only from the sick goat. The veterinary service will give you the correct medication.

per_item.reference: Your goats are suffering from peste des petits ruminants (PPR). Isolate every sick animal at once and stop all movement in and out of the herd. Do not sell or slaughter any animals for market during the outbreak and dispose of carcasses safely. Give the sick animals water and soft feed to support them. Vaccinate all healthy and in-contact animals with PPR vaccine on veterinary advice. Notify the veterinary service immediately.

history.content: My goats have fever and a thick discharge from their noses and eyes.
Do you also see sores inside the mouth or coughing in the affected animals?
Yes, they have sores in the mouth and some are coughing.

draws.answer: The disease is leucaena poisoning, not a bacterial infection. First cut the leucaena back so it forms only about a quarter to a third of the total ration and never let it be the main feed. Then mix the leucaena with grasses and cereal crop residues to give the rumen enough roughage. Introduce the new feed mix slowly over several days, and always provide clean water and a mineral or salt source. If the fever, appetite loss, swelling of the throat, or bloody or brownish urine appear, see the veterinary service.

Your goats are affected by African swine fever. Confine all your goats and stop any movement of animals on or off the place, and keep all outside visitors away from the pen. Disinfect the pen thoroughly and install a footbath at the entrance. Boil any food scraps before feeding them to the sick animals. Dispose of any dead goats by burying or burning them, and never sell or eat a sick animal. Notify the veterinary service immediately because the disease is notifiable and they will guide you on containment.

per_item.reference: This is PPR. Isolate every sick animal right away and stop all movement in and out of the herd. history.content: My goats are showing fever and a muco-purulent discharge from their nose and eyes. What should I do?

draws.answer: You must isolate every surviving animal from the sick ones and avoid moving, selling or gifting any animal. Burn or bury the dead animals and the soiled litter, then disinfect the house. Give the herd a vaccination against nagana as the main disease. For the wet form, see the veterinary service.

This is a sign of leucaena poisoning, not a tick-borne disease. Reduce the leucaena in the diet to only about a quarter to a third of the total ration and never let it become the main feed. Mix the leucaena with grasses and cereal crop residues to provide enough roughage for the rumen. Introduce any feed changes slowly over several days. Ensure the goats always have clean water and a mineral or salt source. If the fever, appetite, or swelling does not improve, contact the veterinary service.

per_item.reference: You should not take cuttings from any plant that shows brown, corky rot inside the roots or yellow leaf-vein blotches, as those are symptoms of cassava brown streak disease. Walk around the area and select only plants that have completely healthy leaves and roots without those signs. Mark those healthy plants and cut stems from them, making sure the variety you choose is known to be tolerant. Do not collect any cuttings from the plants with the brown interior or yellow veins. Remove and destroy the affected plants immediately to avoid spreading the disease. Use the cuttings from the tolerant, symptom-free plants for your planting. ITRA can confirm whether the disease is present if you are unsure.

history.content: My neighbor says his cassava looks fine, but I see some brown spots inside the roots when I pull them up. Can I take cuttings from his field?

draws.answer: No, you should not take cuttings from that field because the brown lesions inside the roots are a sign of cassava bacterial blight. Remove and destroy every cassava plant that has those lesions. Disinfect your tools before you move to the next plant to avoid spreading the bacterium. After you clean your tools, obtain cuttings only from plants that show no disease symptoms. Plant a resistant cassava variety and rotate the plot for the next season. For clean resistant cuttings you can go to ITRA or a registered producer, and ICAT can confirm the diagnosis.

No, do not take cuttings from that field. Brown or pink necrotic spots in the roots, combined with wilting, mean cassava bacterial blight is present. Use only cuttings that come from plants with no signs of these symptoms. Pull out and destroy every cassava plant showing the necrotic root signs. Disinfect your tools between each plant. Plant a resistant variety and rotate the plot. For clean resistant cuttings you can go to ITRA or a registered producer, and ICAT can confirm the diagnosis.

per_item.reference: That weed is Striga, so pull it by hand before it flowers and burn the whole plant to stop seed spread. After removing the weed, spread organic manure and a small amount of urea on the soil to weaken any remaining Striga and help your sorghum grow. history.content: I see a purple flowered weed around the base of my short sorghum plants, what should I do?

draws.answer: That weed is a nitrogen need, not a disease. Look at the leaves; the purple-flowered Striga that grows around the base of short sorghum plants needs nitrogen. Bring back organic matter by applying manure, compost, or leaving residues in the soil rather than burning them. Plant a legume like cowpea, groundnut or soybean in rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. Ask ICAT for a soil analysis and the correct fertilizer dose for your plot.

The purple-flowered Striga is a parasitic weed that hampers the growth of your short sorghum. Pull out the entire Striga plant right at the soil surface from the plot where your sorghum is sown. After that, make sure the sorghum field is free of Striga before you plant the next season. You can obtain methods for controlling Striga and any other weeds on the field.

history.content: My cassava field has leaves with pale yellow mottling and the leaves are twisted and shrunken. Should I treat it as mosaic disease and how?

draws.answer: It is not cassava mosaic disease, it is cassava bacterial blight. The two look different: mosaic shows leaf deformation without angular water-soaked spots, while bacterial blight shows angular water-soaked spots, wilting of young leaves and sometimes gum on stems. Because it is bacterial blight, you must use cuttings only from healthy plants. Remove and destroy any affected plants. Disinfect your tools between plants. Plant a resistant variety and rotate the plot. See ITRA or a registered producer for clean cuttings and ICAT to confirm the diagnosis.

Those signs are cassava mosaic disease, not bacterial blight. Mosaic disease shows leaf deformation with yellow or pale mottling and no wilting, while bacterial blight shows angular water-soaked spots, wilting of young leaves, shoot die-back, and sometimes gum on stems. Because it is mosaic, you must uproot and destroy the strongly mottled, stunted plants. When you plant again, take cuttings only from healthy-looking plants and use a tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer. Avoid any cuttings from mottled or deformed stems. For clean tolerant cuttings, ITRA is the place to go.

per_item.reference: What I can tell you is that you should uproot and destroy any plants showing yellow blotches on the veins or brown corky rot in the roots, and you must not carry cuttings from those areas because the virus spreads on infected cuttings and by whitefly. After removal, plant only cuttings from healthy plants and choose a tolerant variety. I cannot give you an exact distance to keep fields apart, and that detail is not something I can provide.

history.content: how far should fields be spaced to avoid spread

draws.answer: Field spacing depends on the crop and the rotation, and I can provide the general rule while you work it out. If you are rotating cereals, maize, sorghum, millet or fonio on the same plot, use a cereal with a grain legume in the rotation, then a cereal with a root or tuber crop, then a legume, then back to the legume. No spacing figure is given for this, so I will not give a distance; the right spacing comes from your local rotation plan, which you can get from ICAT. For the specific spacing for your maize or sorghum variety, go to ICAT.

The spacing depends on the crop and the rotation, and I must tell you which one you are planting. If you are referring to maize, the guidance is to widen the spacing between rows when growing on depleted ferralsol or when using a tolerant variety against maize streak virus. If you are planting cowpea, the recommendation is to use extra-early varieties with rows 60-65 cm apart and pockets 40 cm apart, or intermediate varieties with rows 80 cm apart and pockets 40 cm apart, and to sow the cowpea mid-June to early July as soon as the rains are strong. If you are planting maize with other crops, the rule is to plant the cereal at the head of the rotation and the legume in the tail, always using the recommended improved tolerant variety.

history.content: I see yellow blotches along the veins of my cassava leaves and the roots turn brown and corky when I pull them up. What actions are required?

draws.answer: Those signs are cassava bacterial blight, so you need to plant a resistant cassava variety and rotate the plot to a different field. Start by selecting cuttings only from plants that have no angular spots, no wilting leaves and no gum on the stems. Then plant those healthy cuttings and cut them at a distance of 5 to 10 cm, never close to the plant. After the new crop, disinfect your pruning tools before you work on the next cassava plant. Pull up any cassava that displays the angular spots, the wilting of young leaves, or the root corkiness and destroy it completely. Never use the same cutting to plant another cassava plant. For clean resistant cuttings you can go to ITRA or a registered producer, and you may ask ICAT to confirm the diagnosis.

Next season, take cuttings only from healthy-looking cassava plants with normal green leaves and no deformation. Plant an improved tolerant cassava variety supplied by ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep the stand uniform and well fed. No spray can cure an infected cassava plant, so remove and destroy the problematic plants immediately. For clean tolerant cuttings, visit ITRA.

per_item.reference: Your cassava has cassava brown streak disease. Use cuttings only from healthy plants and choose a tolerant variety for new planting. history.content: Can I blend two insecticide products together to boost the spray strength?

draws.answer: No, and this is not a question I answer. Insecticide blends do not work the same way, and mixing two products together does not make one stronger: the active ingredient travels in the wrong direction, and the solvency of the mix depends on how well the two mix together, not on the strength. What does work is the strength of the formulation you put in your hand, and the timing of each application. Take the product to ICAT, who will tell you which insecticide is currently approved for your crop and at what rate.

No, you cannot mix the two products. The 2018 ESFT compendium states that a mixture of two or more insecticides has no advantage and that the rate of mixing is not specified, so it does not say which products to combine. What does say is that for any product, the label has the approved product and its rate, and it must be used as instructed. If you want a product that is stronger against your problem, take the product name and its rate to ICAT.

history.content: My field shows cassava leaves that are yellow and twisted, but I also notice some brown rot in the roots. Which disease am I dealing with?

draws.answer: You are facing cassava bacterial blight. First, pull out all cassava plants that are affected and destroy them. Then, for the new planting, cut only from cassava that shows normal green leaves and no deformation or wilting. Use the cuttings for the next season, making sure to clean each tool before you use it on the field. Finally, plant a resistant cassava variety and rotate the plot to another location. For clean resistant cuttings you should contact an ITRA agent or a registered producer.

Those symptoms point to cassava bacterial blight, not cassava mosaic disease. Use only cuttings from plants that have no angular spots, no wilting, and no gum on the stems. Remove and destroy any plant that displays the angular spots and the bacterium. Disinfect your tools between each plant you handle. Plant a resistant cassava variety in the next cycle and rotate the plot to reduce spread. For clean resistant cuttings you should contact ITRA or a registered producer.

per_item.reference: Striga hermonthica is the witchweed that appears as a purple/pink flowered weed at the base of stunted sorghum. Pull the weed by hand before it flowers and burn the uprooted material so the seed does not spread. history.content: What steps should I take to manage Striga hermonthica in my sorghum crop?

draws.answer: Striga hermonthica is the parasitic weed that takes nutrients from sorghum, so you must control it. Sow certified seed that has been treated against damping-off. Weed the sorghum at 2 weeks and again at about 3 weeks after emergence. After harvest, cut the Striga plants at ground level and leave them in the soil to feed the soil fungi that break them down. Then plant a cereal in the same field to take advantage of the nitrogen they left. For the best seed, contact ICAT/Sotouboua seed farm.

Striga hermonthica is the parasitic plant that takes root in sorghum (fingering) during flowering, so you must avoid planting sorghum on the same plot two years in a row and use a legume such as cowpea or soybean. When the plants are young, drop a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each funnel; one kilogram treats about 1,500-2,000 plants and you must repeat this every eight to ten days. Never apply neem powder alone because the oil can scorch the crop, always use the sand or clay carrier. After harvest, destroy or deep-bury the old stalks and plant a cereal in the field. If you need a large outbreak treated area, see ICAT for sanctioned powder and its rate.

per_item.reference: It is not nutrient deficiency, it is Striga, the parasitic weed that attaches to roots and robs the plant. Nutrient deficiency shows no attached weed, while Striga appears as a purple or pink-flowered weed clinging around the base of stunted plants. Because it is Striga, you must pull the weeds by hand before they flower and burn them to stop seed spread. After removal, add organic manure plus some urea, then earth up the soil. Finally, rotate or intercrop with a grain legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean to reduce the seed bank. For tolerant varieties and a rotation plan, consult ICAT.

history.content: My sorghum has Striga, it must be nutrient deficiency, so I just add fertilizer

draws.answer: It is not Striga, it is infestations by Lovecraftia or Asphodelus, which look different. Striga is a plant that wraps around a stem, often green, around a maize stem, and is not a parasite. Lovecraftia and Asphodelus appear in tzotZot and are not parasites; the two you described are not the same insect. For Striga you should pull it out before it sets flowers, not treat for a nutrient deficiency. If you later see a dead-heart, that is the insect that does that, not a nutrient need. See ICAT for control.

It is not Striga, it is Cercospora leaf-spot fungi that make the pale streaks along the veins and reduce yield. Striga is a parasitic plant that attaches to cereal stalks and is solved by not growing on the same land year after year, using a cereal rotation, and removing Striga with a pinch of groundnut, cotton or soybean seed. For the nutrient deficiency you see, you should first look at the leaves: yellowing that begins on the old lower leaves while the young top leaves stay green indicates nitrogen shortage, not Striga. Then, on a soil test rather than on a broad-spectrum NPK, you apply the right amount of nitrogen. Also avoid a large portion of the legume, cut the stems at ground level, and keep the soil unbroken. Finally, see ICAT for a soil check and the dose for your plot.

history.content: I see a pink-flowered weed clinging to the base of my sorghum and the plants look short. What should I do?

You can see ICAT for the correct variety for your region.

The weed is straw, and you must pull it out before the sorghum flowers. Weed the field about two weeks after sowing and then do the first weeding without breaking the ridges. When you reach panicle initiation, apply the estimated 20-25 kg of NPK fertilizer per hectare, plus urea at 100 kg per hectare. Protect the sorghum from birds by placing netting 10-15 cm above the plants and keeping the field clear of weeds. For matching a variety to your local rain pattern, visit ICAT.

history.content: how stop Striga seed buildup

draws.answer: Do not grow your maize on the same plot for more than two seasons in a row, because maize streak virus stays in the plant's roots. First, plant a cereal or legume crop and cut the stems at ground level, leaving the nitrogen-fixing root nodules in the soil. Second, pull out any Striga plants that appear, usually from your field. Third, plant a Striga-infested cereal or legume early, as early sowing prevents the virus from arriving. If you need confirmation of the disease or help choosing a tolerant variety, go to ICAT.

Remove Striga from the field before it flowers. Striga grows on the stem of the legume plants and its root-like organs suck the nutrients from the plant, so you must pull it out at the first sign of flower, which is usually early in the season. Also plant a cereal on the same plot to compete for the light and the resources left by Striga. If you need help telling the two apart, go to ICAT for confirmation.

history.content: My sorghum is very stunted and I notice a pink-flowered weed at the base, how can I manage it?

draws.answer: The pink-flowered Striga weed grows on the base of sorghum plants and competes for nutrients and water. Begin by recognising the weed's presence before any crop is cut. Pull the entire Striga plant from the sorghum field as soon as you identify it. Then, at the first signs of sorghum stunting, pause from a legume crop and rotate the plot with a cereal. Use a cereal variety that matures in 55-75 days and sow it when the rains are strong, typically from mid-June to early July. Keep the field weed-free from mid-June to early July for the Striga to have less space. For advice on the best variety for your area, see ICAT.

The pink-flowered Striga is a parasitic weed that must be removed before the sorghum flowers. Sow your sorghum on ridges after a heavy rain, placing 3-5 seeds per pocket at 3-5 cm depth and using 6-8 kg per hectare of treated seed. Three weeks later perform the first weeding, then apply NPK at 150-200 kg per hectare, followed by urea at 50-100 kg per hectare and earth up against lodging. Before flowering, pull any Striga plants that appear near the sorghum. If you need help matching a variety to your region, see ICAT.

history.content: Would mixing two different insecticides give a stronger spray?

draws.answer: No, mixing two insecticides does not make it stronger. The approved product and its rate are written on the container itself, and mixing alters the number of chemicals you are applying, not the power of the one you have. Inspect the label before any mixing, and follow the dosage accurately. If the pest problem keeps coming back, ask ICAT for a product suitable for your crop.

No, and there is a reason to believe it is not. When two or more products sit on a crop, the active ingredients do not meet up. The Ministry of Agriculture, citing ITRA and PASA, says that mixing different products on a crop produces no more active substance than applying them alone, and it warns against the use of a combination for protection, which costs more money and may leave residues on fruit. The reason is not just mixing it, it is that the two compounds have different properties: one is the active ingredient, the other is the carrier, and they work in different ways. So the strongest product you use is not the one the label says.

history.content: My sheep are dying fast from a disease that looks like PPR, what steps save the rest?

draws.answer: It is leucaena poisoning, not scabsiform leucaena poisoning. First, cut the leucaena back so it makes up only a quarter to a third of the total ration. Second, replace the removed leucaena with grasses and cereal crop residues to provide more roughage. Third, introduce the new feed gradually over several days. Fourth, keep clean water available and give a mineral or salt source. If the sheep keep dying despite these steps, see the veterinary service.

It is not only Pappia or Bactria; it is also the common tick-borne disease called gall sickness. First, hand-pick all visible ticks from every animal in the herd, not only the sick one. Remove ticks from ears, under the tail and between the legs. Then call the veterinary service the same day so they can confirm the disease and give the correct drug and dose. Tell the vet the urine colour: yellow-brown without red points to gall sickness. Keep the sick sheep in the shade, give it clean water, and avoid making it walk. Never reuse a needle on another animal. The veterinary service will provide the proper treatment.

history.content: My sorghum is stunted and I notice a pink-flowered plant wrapping its stems near the ground. How can I manage this?

draws.answer: Pink-flowered stunting with a wrapped stem is typical of groundnut rosette. First, pull out and destroy every plant that shows severe stunting, yellowing or bunched, green leaves, or are buried. Then, for the next season, sow your groundnut early and at the recommended close spacing, as dense early stands suffer far less. Keep the field weed-free to reduce aphid hosts. Plant a tolerant variety next season. For resistant varieties, go to ICAT.

The pink-flowered stunting plant is a sign of groundnut rosette, a virus spread by aphids. Start by rogueing out and destroying the severely affected plants to cut the source. Next, sow your next crop early and use the recommended close spacing, because dense early stands suffer far less. Keep the field weed-free to reduce alternative aphid hosts. Finally, plant a tolerant variety for the next season. To obtain resistant varieties, go to ICAT.

per_item.reference: Those symptoms point to PPR, peste des petits ruminants, a fast and highly contagious virus affecting goats. First, isolate every sick goat together and halt all animal movements into or out of the herd. You must not sell or slaughter any goats for market during this outbreak, and any carcasses must be disposed of safely. Provide the sick goats with water and soft feed to support them. After that, vaccinate all healthy and in-contact goats with the PPR vaccine on veterinary advice. Notify the veterinary service IMMEDIATELY.

history.content: All my goats are running a fever, their eyes and noses are full of pus, and a few have died already.

draws.answer: That is a tick-borne disease, gall sickness, affecting the red blood cells, and it is redwater. Call the veterinary service today; they alone can identify the disease and prescribe the right drug and its dose. Tell the vet the colour of the urine, red to black means redwater, yellow-brown without red means gall sickness, and it is red for redwater. Keep the sick goat in the shade, provide clean water, and avoid making it walk because it is short of red blood cells. Hand-pick every tick you can see on all your cattle, not just the sick one, since ticks on the others can spread the parasite. Do not use the same needle on two animals because gall sickness can travel on a contaminated needle. See the veterinary service the same day.

Your goats are afflicted by gall sickness, which is caused by Anaplasma marginale. Call the veterinary service the same day so they can diagnose and provide the correct drug and dose. Tell the vet the colour of the urine; yellow-brown points to gall sickness, red urine points to redwater. Keep the sick goats in shade, give them clean water and prevent them from walking. Remove any ticks you see on the whole herd, not only on the sick goat. The veterinary service will give you the proper treatment.

history.content: How much urea should I mix with manure to control Striga on my sorghum?

draws.answer: You should use about 100 kg of urea per hectare together with the manure, which is roughly 50 kg for your 0.25 ha field. First, sow a sorghum stalk at 80-100 cm, doing the first weeding 2-3 times while the plants are small. Then, during the crop's second wave, insert the urea-manure mix at the tillering stage, placing it in a pocket 5-10 cm from each root node and keeping it away from the seedling. Keep the second weeding without breaking the pocket. Avoid any extra-early sorghum sowing because it leaves the plant vulnerable to Striga. For variety matching or exact rate advice, go to ICAT.

You should first confirm that the plant is showing stunted bushy growth on the stem and rogue out and destroy the worst-affected plants to cut the source of the fungus. Then, for the next season, plant a cereal in the same field and rotate the plot to a legume such as cowpea or soybean, using the recommended nitrogen-fixing practice. I cannot give you the exact urea amount, but you can obtain a precise calculation from ICAT.

per_item.reference: The twisted leaves indicate cassava mosaic disease, while the brown corky rot inside the roots points to cassava brown streak disease. For the cassava mosaic disease plants, uproot and destroy the strongly mottled and stunted ones. Then, for the next planting, take cuttings only from healthy-looking cassava mosaic disease plants and never from a deformed stem. Plant an improved tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and keep the stand uniform and well-fed. history.content: My field has some cassava with twisted leaves and others with brown rot inside the roots. Which problem am I dealing with?

draws.answer: I cannot name it from those signs, because both cassava mosaic disease and cassava bacterial blight are solved by distinct things and I have no way to tell them apart from them once they appear. Mosaic gives yellow mottling, leaf deformation, stunted growth and sometimes yellow or pale streaks along veins, and bacterial blight gives angular water-soaked spots on the leaves, wilting of young leaves, shoot die-back and sometimes gum on stems. What you describe is not what I was taught, so I have nothing to give you to match it. For any of the two, isolate the affected plants, destroy them, and destroy any cuttings from them. Use cuttings only from healthy plants, and choose a tolerant variety from ITRA or a registered cutting producer.

The symptoms point to cassava mosaic disease. Uproot and destroy the cassava plants that are strongly mottled and stunted. When you plant again, cut only from cassava plants that have normal green leaves and no deformation. Obtain improved tolerant cuttings from ITRA or a registered cutting producer and plant them together with your regular cassava varieties. Maintain a uniform, well-fed cassava stand. If you need clean tolerant cuttings, ITRA can provide them.

history.content: I found a pink flower weed hugging the bottom of my short sorghum stalks, what steps should I take?

draws.answer: That weed is strawchoke, and you must remove it immediately to keep the field clean. First, cut the plants at ground level and bury them so the nitrogen-fixing roots stay in the soil. Then, when you plant your sorghum again, put a legume like cowpea, groundnut or soybean into the rotation and cut its stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules remain in the soil. Do not guess a pesticide or fertilizer dose because mineral fertilizer alone often does not pay back on depleted soil. Finally, see ICAT for a soil analysis and the correct fertilizer dose for your plot.

The pink-flowered Striga is a parasitic weed that attaches itself to sorghum, and you must pull it out before it flowers. First, look at your sorghum plants; when the flowers are still small, pull out any Striga clinging to the base. Then, at the first sign of flowering, cut the Striga plants off them and toss them away. Keep the sorghum field free of Striga from other plants you clear in the area. After you cut the Striga, rotate or intercrop the sorghum with a legume such as cowpea or soybean. For any questions about sorghum varieties or whether a spray is needed, contact ICAT.

history.content: My sorghum is very stunted and I notice a pink weed clinging to its base, how can I fix this?

draws.answer: The problem is stalk borer on sorghum, which shows window-pane holes in the whorl leaves and a dead-heart with swollen, bristled stalks. While the crop is young, drop a pinch of ground neem-seed powder mixed 1:1 with dry sand or clay into each funnel; one kilogram treats about 1,500-2,000 plants and you need to repeat the application every 8-10 days. Never apply neem powder alone because the oil can scorch the plant. After harvest, destroy or deep-bury the old stalks and rotate or intercrop with a legume such as cowpea or soybean. If a large area is affected at once, see ICAT quickly for approved control.

The problem is chili pepper, strawberry or gboma, growing in your sorghum. First, sow a resistant sorghum variety that matures in 55-75 days and conduct the first weeding about two weeks after sowing. About a week later place the chili pepper seeds in a separate pocket, 3-5 cm apart, with the seeds at a depth of 2-3 cm and stake them. Do not grow sorghum on the same plot for more than two years; rotate with a legume such as cowpea or soybean. Later harvest the sorghum at the proper stage, between 15-25 days, and perform the first weeding without breaking the chili pockets. For a variety suited to sorghum and any pest concerns, contact ICAT.

On veterinary advice, vaccinate all healthy and in-contact animals with PPR vaccine. Notify the veterinary service immediately.

history.content: How do I manage an outbreak of peste des petits ruminants in my flock?

draws.answer: The disease is called a tick-borne illness. First, stop letting any animal graze in riverine bush during the biting hours and find alternative pastures. Keep the herd well fed and watered to support the immune system. Next, report the case to the veterinary service so they can identify the disease and give the right trypanocide. Finally, avoid using the same injection needle on more than one animal. For accurate diagnosis and treatment, see the veterinary service.

The disease is called a tick-borne infection. First, isolate every animal that is still alive from the sick ones and do not move, sell or give any bird away. Then burn or bury the dead animals and any soiled litter and disinfect the pen. After that, vaccinate the remaining herd with the La Sota or B1 strain in the drinking water or as an eye-drop, and repeat the vaccination on the recommended schedule. Contact the veterinary service or your village livestock auxiliary right away.

history.content: My cassava roots look brown and corky when I harvest them, could it be the same as bacterial blight?

draws.answer: The brown corky rot on cassava roots is caused by African cassava brown streak disease, which is transmitted by whitefly. First, pull out and destroy any cassava plant that displays the symptoms. Then, when you plant your next cassava crop, cut only from cassava plants that have normal green leaves and no leaf deformation. Do not cut from a any plant that shows the brown corky rot. After you plant, plant a resistant cassava variety and rotate the plot for the next season. To obtain clean resistant cuttings, go to ITRA or a registered producer.

Yes, cassava brown streak disease can cause roots that are brown and corky when harvested. First, pull out and destroy any plant with those symptoms. Next, for the new planting, cut only from plants that have normal green leaves and no streaks. Then plant a resistant cassava variety and rotate the plot to a new area. For clean cuttings you should contact an ITRA or a registered producer.

history.content: Can I mix two insecticides in one spray to make it stronger?

draws.answer: No, and mixing two insecticides together does not make them stronger. When you put two products on a plant, you are putting two substances in contact with each other, and the plant has no way of distinguishing which one is the active ingredient. The spray acts on the pest in different ways, so the pest can leave even when a part of the plant remains coated. If you think a combination will work better, go to ICAT for an approved product and its rate; mixing a product does not change the rate.

No, and it is worth repeating the rule on its own. Mixing two insecticides in one spray does not make it stronger: the active ingredient is already there in a different form, and the solution is still a solution. What changes is the way you finish the job, not the concentration. The label says to spray when the insects are still present, that is as soon as you see them, and to repeat the application every eight to ten days. A stronger product would still need those five actions, and a weak product would not. If you are unsure which product to use, ask ICAT; they can see the crop and give the approved product and its rate.

history.content: My herd of goats started coughing and their eyes are running pus. What must I do right now?

draws.answer: Your goats are showing signs of leucaena poisoning because leucaena makes them drool and they can hardly walk, and the problem is worse when leucaena makes up too large a share of their ration. Cut the leucaena back so it is only a quarter to a third of the total feed and never the main ingredient. Mix the remaining leucaena with grasses and cereal crop residues to give the rumen plenty of roughage. Change the feed composition slowly over several days, keeping clean water and a mineral or salt source always available. If the goats keep refusing food, keep moving, or you see drooling or a swollen throat, go to the veterinary service.

You must call the veterinary service the same day because they are the only ones who can identify the disease and prescribe the correct drug and dose. Inform the vet about the urine colour, since red to black indicates redwater and yellow-brown without red indicates gall sickness. history.content: I have cassava brown streak disease in my field. What should I do to stop it spreading?

draws.answer: Use cuttings only from healthy plants. First, walk the field and identify any plants that have yellow or pale mottling and twisted, puckered leaves. Uproot and destroy those affected plants. After each plant, disinfect your cutting tools before moving to the next one. Only take cuttings from plants that show no problems. Then plant a resistant cassava variety in the cleared area and rotate the plot for the next season. For clean resistant cuttings you can go to ITRA or a registered producer, and ICAT can help confirm the disease.

Use cuttings only from healthy plants. history.content: I have sorghum that stays short and yellow, and a purple weed clings to its base, what is the cause?

draws.answer: The problem is Striga, a parasitic plant that binds to cereals and reduces the harvest. After the legumes are harvested, sow a cereal crop and cut the Striga plants at the soil surface. Then rotate the plot for the next season and ask ICAT for a legume recommendation that suits your area.

history.content: my sorghum looks yellow because of nutrient deficiency, right?

draws.answer: No, that is not a nutrient problem. Yellowing that starts on the OLD lower leaves and climbs, with the youngest leaves still green, is a nitrogen shortage, not a disease. The signs appear gradually over several years as the plant moves nitrogen to the young leaves, and there is no specific fertilizer or dose to guess. Do not buy a broad-spectrum NPK or a systemic fungicide on a merchant's word, because on depleted soil the mineral fertilizer alone often does not pay off. First bring organic matter back with manure, compost, or unburned residues. Then add a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. Ask ICAT for a soil analysis and the correct dose for your plot.

history.content: My herd has sudden diarrhoea and many goats are dying quickly, almost all of them. What is happening?

draws.answer: It is leucaena poisoning caused by excessive leucaena in the diet. Cut the leucaena back to a supplement, about a quarter to a third of the total ration, and never let it become the main feed. Mix the leucaena with grasses and cereal crop residues to provide enough roughage for the rumen. Introduce any feed change gradually over several days. Keep clean water and a mineral or salt source always available. If the goats keep dying even after you have reduced leucaena, see the veterinary service.

history.content: My cassava leaves have yellow streaks on the veins and when I dig up the roots they are brown and corky. What should I do?

draws.answer: Those signs point to cassava bacterial blight, so use only cuttings taken from healthy plants. Remove and destroy every cassava plant that is infected with the disease. Disinfect your cutting tools after each plant you handle. Plant a resistant cassava variety in the cleared area and rotate the plot to another site later. For clean resistant cuttings you can go to ITRA or a registered producer, and ICAT can help confirm the diagnosis.

Those signs indicate cassava mosaic disease, which cannot be cured with spray. Remove and destroy any plants that show strong yellow mottling or mottling together with twisted, puckered or shrunken leaves. For the next planting, select cuttings only from plants that look healthy and have no mottling, no deformation and no gum on the stems. Avoid using cuttings from any plant that was already infected. Plant an improved tolerant variety that you can obtain from ITRA or a registered cutting producer. Ensure you have a clean cutting tool for each plant you handle.

history.content: What steps should I take against Striga hermonthica on my sorghum?

draws.answer: Striga hermonthica is the parasitic plant that takes over the lodging of your sorghum plants. First, check the base of each stalk daily and pull out the striga plants before the sorghum flowers. Second, sow your sorghum on ridges after a heavy rain, placing three to five grains per pocket at three to five centimetres depth and using six to eight kilograms of treated seed per hectare. Third, thin the sorghum to two or three plants where you see six to eight plants down to two or three plants. Fourth, manage any remaining striga by burning or deep-burying the stalks at ground level. Finally, consult ICAT for the currently approved product and exact dose.

Striga hermonthica is the parasitic weed of sorghum that you must avoid by sowing early and at the recommended density, using a tolerant variety, and controlling weeds early. First, sow your sorghum on ridges after a heavy rain, placing 3 to 5 grains per pocket at 3 to 5 grams per pocket, and use 6 to 8 weeks for emergence. Second, perform the first weeding 10 to 15 days after sowing. Third, apply the Top-down strategy of fertiliser application at 150 to 200 grams per hectare, followed by urea at 50 to 100 grams per hectare and a pinch of ground neem-seed powder at each flowering stage. If an early infestation of Striga appears, go to ICAT for the right variety.
